title: Allahabad HC Splits on Bulldozer Ban, Slams India's 'Normalised Corruption'
excerpt: Justice Atul Sreedharan proposed a two-year ban on demolishing homes of accused persons, citing the Ram Temple donation theft as the 'nadir of Indian integrity,' but co-judge Justice Siddharth Nandan called the restrictions 'unwarranted judicial activism.'
body:
• A division bench of the Allahabad High Court delivered a split verdict on "bulldozer justice," with Justice Atul Sreedharan proposing a two-year ban on demolishing homes after an FIR is filed and Justice Siddharth Nandan rejecting it as judicial overreach.
  • Justice Sreedharan cited the Ram Temple donation theft in Ayodhya as evidence of India's deeply entrenched corruption, suggesting the death penalty for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
  • Both judges agreed that demolishing an accused person's home under the guise of municipal law enforcement is a "retributive exercise of executive discretion" and an illegal abuse of power.
  • The ruling stems from a case in which a Hamirpur family's properties were targeted by authorities shortly after a relative was booked under the POCSO Act.

A division bench of the Allahabad High Court delivered a sharply divided ruling on Monday on the practice of "bulldozer justice" in Uttar Pradesh, with one judge calling for sweeping restrictions on state-led demolitions and the other warning against what he termed judicial overreach.

In a 51-page opinion, Justice Atul Sreedharan proposed that no action be taken to demolish the home of a person accused of an offence for two years from the date of FIR registration. He argued the hiatus would allow the state's urge to "satiate the presumable public anger" to dissipate before any demolition proceeds. Justice Siddharth Nandan, writing a separate 24-page judgment, firmly dissented, calling the proposed restrictions "unwarranted judicial activism" that would encroach upon the legislature's domain.

A Case from Hamirpur

The verdict arose from a writ petition filed by a Hamirpur family whose properties were targeted by authorities shortly after a relative was booked under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO), the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the IT Act, and the UP Prohibition of Unlawful Religious Conversion Act. The family alleged the demolition action was punitive rather than a genuine exercise of municipal enforcement.

Justice Sreedharan opened his judgment with a couplet by Urdu poet Bashir Badr: "People face ruination in just making a home, and you feel no remorse setting ablaze entire settlements." He characterized the immediate demolition of an accused's dwelling as a "retributive exercise of executive discretion" — identifying it as the "vilest species" of colourable exercise of executive power.

Ram Temple Theft and the 'Nadir of Integrity'

Going beyond the bulldozer issue, Justice Sreedharan delivered a broader indictment of corruption in Indian institutions. He cited the recent theft of donations at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya as evidence that dishonesty has become deeply normalized across society.

"The recent controversy relating to the theft of donations at the Ram Temple is the proverbial last straw on the camel's back. Nothing can shame a people who remain unfazed by the theft at the Ram Temple which epitomises the nadir of the Indian's integrity."

— Justice Atul Sreedharan, Allahabad High Court

He noted that India ranks 91 among 182 nations in the Transparency International 2025 report, remarking that "it does not shame us." He warned that unchecked corruption would lead to the illicit concentration of wealth, "widening the chasm between the haves and the have-nots" and laying "the script for civil unrest in days to come."

In what may be his most radical proposal, Justice Sreedharan urged the state to consider amending the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, to introduce the death penalty for those convicted of corruption.

Where the Judges Agreed — and Diverged

Both judges concurred that when the state acts maliciously to target an accused's property under the guise of municipal law, it constitutes an illegal abuse of power. They also agreed that if demolition notices are issued for construction violations, simultaneous proceedings under the Prevention of Corruption Act must be initiated against erring municipal and police officers who allowed the structures to be built, with those proceedings concluded within six months.

The disagreement centered on Justice Sreedharan's three proposed restrictions. Beyond the two-year hiatus, he directed that authorities must give one year's advance notice before initiating eviction of residents who have occupied structures for three or more years, with a waiver allowed only in cases of "compelling urgency." Justice Nandan rejected all three proposals, warning that a blanket two-year embargo would keep the UP Urban Planning and Development Act in abeyance and could encourage the filing of "frivolous FIRs" to shield illegal constructions.

"The State is certain that the society suffers from collective schadenfreude and shall applaud the State for dispensing vigilante-style summary justice, without adhering to the procedure established by law."

— Justice Atul Sreedharan, Allahabad High Court

Defying the Supreme Court

Justice Sreedharan highlighted that bulldozer demolitions continue across Uttar Pradesh despite the Supreme Court's 2025 guidelines restricting punitive demolitions. "The demolitions continue with impunity as though these judgments do not exist, or the State is certain that the defiance towards the law laid down by the highest Court of the land shall not visit them with any adverse consequences," he observed.

He also pointed to the complicity of the state apparatus, noting that no unauthorized structure "comes up overnight" and that officials who allow illegal construction — often in exchange for bribes — bear responsibility. The state, he said, becomes particeps criminis, an accomplice, by providing sovereign amenities like water and electricity to unauthorized structures while later demolishing them.

What Happens Next

With the division bench split, the matter will likely be referred to a larger bench of the Allahabad High Court for a final determination. The case, Faimuddeen and 2 others v. State of U.P. and 7 others, could set significant precedent on the limits of executive power in demolition actions across India. The ruling arrives as "bulldozer justice" remains a politically charged issue in multiple Indian states, with civil liberties organizations and opposition parties arguing the demolitions disproportionately target marginalized communities.
